clue.text: Victorian chimney sweeping, an example of nepotism?

definitions.text: Victorian chimney sweeping, an example of nepotism?

parts.words: Victorian chimney sweeping, an example of nepotism
parts.note: Victorian sweeps sent small boys up the flues, so the trade literally offered work for lads; the phrase usually means posts handed to cronies

explanation.surface: A social historian wonders whether the Victorian practice of child chimney sweeps counted as favouritism.
explanation.walkthrough: The usual sense is posts given to friends or relatives; the clue reads it literally, since Victorian sweeps employed small boys to climb chimneys.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for nepotism: lucrative posts handed to friends and insiders rather than earned.

clue.text: One that's booked by ref — not good, but he is confused with score

indicators.note: not good means the letter for good is dropped from the word for ref

parts.note: a referee is a judge of play

indicators.note: is confused tells us the letters of but he and score are jumbled together

explanation.surface: A football referee who has lost his touch gets muddled about the score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'booked by ref' looks like a football caution; in fact the definition is 'One that's booked', a title found in a book. 'not good' takes G from JUDGE to leave JUDE; 'is confused' rearranges BUTHESCORE.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy's novel, so its title is literally something put between book covers.

clue.text: In north-west town finally executing pirate

parts.note: Bootle is a town on Merseyside in north-west England

indicators.note: finally picks out the closing letter of the word executing

explanation.surface: A pirate is put to death at last in a town in the north-west of England.
explanation.walkthrough: BOOTLE is a town near Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: To pirate goods, recordings or drink is to produce or sell them illicitly, which is bootlegging.

clue.text: Ditch supporting comic, clarifying this is not peculiar

indicators.note: in a down light, the supporting piece sits underneath the other

parts.note: comic and funny are synonyms
a ha-ha is a sunken ditch serving as a fence on country estates

explanation.surface: A comedian propped up by a ditch somehow explains that something is not odd.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is half of the pair 'funny peculiar or funny ha-ha?', used to say which sense of funny is meant. A ha-ha is a landscaped boundary trench.
explanation.definitionFit: Speakers add this tag to show that by funny they mean amusing rather than strange.

clue.text: Have new concerns about defensive position

definitions.meaning: to ... is to doubt once more, taking up fresh worries
a fortification or stronghold held against attack

explanation.surface: A soldier starts to worry again about the fortified spot being held.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense splits the word as RE-DOUBT, to doubt anew; 'about' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A redoubt is a small fortified outwork or stronghold, a classic defensive position.

clue.text: Wooden moves by husband in dance

indicators.note: by means placed next to, so the husband letter sits beside the rearranged word
moves tells us the letters of Wooden shift into a new order

explanation.surface: A husband dances stiffly, his moves wooden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moves' rearranges WOODEN as OEDOWN.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoedown is a lively American country dance, or the social gathering where it happens.

clue.text: Bravo! Manage to circle Mars

parts.note: Bravo is B in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to manage a business is to run it
a circle has the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: Cheers for a plan to orbit the red planet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mars' looks like the planet but is the pop singer Bruno Mars.
explanation.definitionFit: The American singer known as Bruno Mars took this first name as a stage name.

clue.text: Hobby is dreadfully uncivilised

indicators.note: dreadfully suggests things done badly, so the letters of Hobby is are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone's pastime is condemned as barbaric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dreadfully' rearranges HOBBYIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A yob is a British loutish youth, so behaviour like his is rough and uncivilised.

clue.text: Take a breather, others working — I progress spectacularly

parts.note: the rest means the others
a machine that is on is working
I as the Roman numeral is one
something that soars rises dramatically

explanation.surface: While everyone else does the work, someone pauses and boasts of their own brilliant advance.
explanation.walkthrough: Each piece is a synonym in clue order; I is read as the number one.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from rowers pausing mid-stroke, means to stop and relax after effort, like taking a break.

clue.text: One way to be dead drunk: swallowing beer at the end

indicators.note: swallowing means one piece takes the other inside it

parts.note: a drink downed is one drunk

indicators.note: at the end picks the closing letter of the word beer

explanation.surface: Being blind drunk, having gulped down beer, is a kind of death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' suggests intoxicated, but here it is a past participle meaning swallowed down, DOWNED, which takes in R from the end of 'beer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Death by water filling the lungs is one particular manner of perishing.

clue.text: Even question being in Europe; from set of data, it's time to leave

indicators.note: being in tells us the question letter goes inside the Europe letters

parts.note: EU is the European Union

indicators.note: to leave says the time letter departs from the data word

parts.note: a table is an array of data

explanation.surface: A calm statistician says a question about Europe is settled and it is time to quit the spreadsheet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' looks like an adverb but is the adjective meaning steady. 'from' marks the word being cut; 'it's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Equable means steady and untroubled, an even temperament or climate.

clue.text: Box like William, the national hero?

parts.note: William Tell is the legendary national hero of Switzerland
the suffix -y means like or characterised by

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a box resembles the Swiss archer of legend.
explanation.walkthrough: Adding -y to a name makes an adjective meaning 'like' it, so TELL plus Y is 'Tell-like'. Box and telly are both British slang for television.
explanation.definitionFit: Box is British slang for a television set, as is telly.

clue.text: Classy old record in handwriting for student of the highest mysteries

parts.note: U means upper-class, as in U and non-U

indicators.note: in places the old record inside the handwriting word

parts.note: fist is slang for a person's handwriting
a log is a written record

explanation.surface: A posh old diary in someone's handwriting belongs to a scholar of the deepest secrets.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the dated label for upper-class usage. 'Fist' meaning handwriting is old-fashioned. The highest mysteries are things in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who studies unidentified flying objects examines puzzles that are literally high up.

clue.text: On short boundary, flyer's not about to go to ground

indicators.note: On means the following pieces are placed after the boundary piece
short means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: an edge is a boundary
BA is British Airways, an airline or flyer, and 's adds S

indicators.note: about means the word not is turned round

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket ball barely clears the rope, and a bird is not about to land.
explanation.walkthrough: EDG is EDGE cut short. BA's gives BAS, and 'about' turns NOT into TON. EDGBASTON is the Test cricket ground in Birmingham.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgbaston is a cricket stadium in Birmingham, and a ground in sport is a venue or stadium.

clue.text: Looking terrified, woman hides in an opening

indicators.note: hides in means the female pronoun is tucked inside the word an

parts.note: she is a pronoun for a woman

explanation.surface: A frightened woman hides inside a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an opening' describes AN being opened up to take SHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashen means pale as ash, the colour a face turns from fear or shock.

clue.text: Primate's one request at first I obey

parts.note: the aye-aye is a Madagascan lemur, a primate; the 's adds S
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: at first picks the opening letter of the word request

explanation.surface: A bishop's single request is met by someone who promises compliance immediately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' suggests an archbishop, but here it is the aye-aye lemur.
explanation.definitionFit: A naval reply to an order meaning yes, I will do it at once.

clue.text: Black bear's pouch

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
Ursa is Latin for bear, as in Ursa Major; the 's is a link meaning is

explanation.surface: A dark-coated bear has a pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bear's' reads as 'bear is', so URSA is followed by the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bursa is an anatomical sac or fluid-filled pocket, such as those cushioning joints.

clue.text: Curious allure about bachelor, spotted with this

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the bachelor letter
curious suggests something odd, so the letters of allure are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bachelor of strange charm is seen to be covered in spots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curious' rearranges ALLURE as RUELLA, which goes 'about' B.
explanation.definitionFit: German measles, a viral illness, produces a red rash, so a sufferer is spotted with it.

clue.text: Antiquated test hard at elite school, they say

parts.note: the MOT is the annual British roadworthiness test for vehicles
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

indicators.note: they say signals that the school's name is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: A tough old exam at a top school is dismissed as out of date.
explanation.walkthrough: ETON, the elite boarding school near Windsor, sounds like EATEN. The MOT is the British vehicle safety test.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes chewed by moths are worn and shabby, hence figuratively outdated or antiquated.

clue.text: Conductor runs in majestically? Not so

indicators.note: in means the runs letter goes inside the trimmed word
Not tells us the letters of the word so are removed

parts.note: maestoso is the musical direction meaning majestically
taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A conductor wonders whether to rush grandly through a passage, and decides against it.
explanation.walkthrough: MAESTOSO is the Italian musical marking for 'majestic'. 'Not so' removes one SO to leave MAESTO, and R goes 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Maestro is the honorific for a distinguished musician, especially an orchestra's conductor.

clue.text: Tramcar to move, although upset about it

indicators.note: about means the turned word goes around the moving word
upset in a down light means the word is turned upside down, reading from bottom to top

parts.note: yet can mean although, as in 'simple yet effective'
to roll is to move along on wheels

explanation.surface: A tram must get going even though someone is cross about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses YET to TEY, which goes 'about' ROLL.
explanation.definitionFit: A trolley car is the American term for a tram, drawing power via an overhead pole.

clue.text: Fear losing gold card in house row

indicators.note: losing means the gold letters are dropped from the fear word

parts.note: terror is extreme fear
OR is the heraldic word for gold
an ace is a playing card

explanation.surface: A gambler's dread of losing his gold and card in a house sits behind the row of homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing gold' takes OR out of TERROR, leaving TERR.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrace is a British row of joined houses built in one continuous block.

clue.text: Intriguing team with new role for Spaniard

parts.note: a cabal is a group of plotters

indicators.note: new suggests a fresh version, so the letters of role are rearranged

explanation.surface: A scheming faction gives a Spaniard a fresh part to play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges ROLE as LERO.
explanation.definitionFit: Caballero is a Spanish gentleman or horseman, so the word fits a man from Spain.

clue.text: Go and wash round back of house

indicators.note: round means the wash word goes around the next letter

parts.note: lave is a literary word for wash

indicators.note: back of picks the final letter of the word house

explanation.surface: Someone is told to depart and clean around the rear of the home.
explanation.walkthrough: LAVE is an old word for wash; it goes 'round' E, the back of 'house'.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave is to go away or depart.

clue.text: Battles to unwrap birthday present

indicators.note: unwrapping strips the outer letters off birthday present, leaving the inside run

explanation.surface: Children squabble over opening a birthday gift.
explanation.walkthrough: Ypres in Belgium gave its name to several First World War battles.
explanation.definitionFit: The Battles of Ypres were a series of major Western Front clashes, named for the Flemish town.

clue.text: Dependent on Robin?

definitions.meaning: the three-wheeled Robin car was made by a British company of that name, so its badge is on every Robin

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person relies on a friend called Robin.
explanation.walkthrough: The Reliant Robin was a British three-wheeled car, its maker's name on the car.
explanation.definitionFit: Being reliant on something means depending on it.

clue.text: Falstaff, maybe, here left drinkers' association imbibing special calories

indicators.note: imbibing means drinking in, so the association letters take the next pieces inside

parts.note: AA is Alcoholics Anonymous, a fellowship for problem drinkers
cal is short for calories

explanation.surface: Fat old Falstaff walked out of a drinking club that was taking in extra calories.
explanation.walkthrough: Falstaff is Verdi's opera, first staged at La Scala in Milan, not just Shakespeare's knight. AA is Alcoholics Anonymous.
explanation.definitionFit: The Milan opera house where Verdi's Falstaff premiered in 1893, so a place it is staged.

clue.text: Wait at priests' table to join them?

definitions.text: Wait at priests' table to join them?

parts.words: Wait at priests' table to join them
parts.note: a waiter at a clergy dinner would take the diners' requests; the same words mean being ordained

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether serving dinner to clergy is the way into the priesthood.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, it is a waiter noting the sacred diners' requests; idiomatically it means being ordained.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to be ordained as a priest or minister, entering the clergy.
